title: Number of Islands
statement: You get a map as a grid of the strings "1" (land) and "0" (water). An island is a group of land cells joined side to side, up, down, left or right. Diagonals do not join. Return how many separate islands the map has.

example.caption: Two groups of land. The cell at (1,1) is joined to (0,1) from below, so the left group is one island. The right group is a second one.

idea.sentence: Scan the map. Each time you meet land that no island owns yet, count one new island and flood outward from it to claim every connected land cell.

jargon.plain: Start at one cell and keep spreading to every connected neighbour of the same kind, like water filling a pond.
Two land cells are connected if you can walk from one to the other over land, moving up, down, left or right.
Depth-first search: follow one neighbour as far as it goes, then come back and try the next. Here a recursive function does it.

watch.inputHint: One argument: the map as rows of "1" and "0" strings, e.g. [["1","0"],["0","1"]]

vars.meaning: number of cells in the map (rows times columns)

compare.bruteLabel: Flood from every land cell and compare the results

rows.name: Flood from every land cell
rows.note: Each flood walks a whole island, and you start one per land cell. You must also merge duplicates.

rows.name: Claim cells while flooding
rows.note: The scan visits each cell once. A flood visits each land cell once. Claimed cells are skipped. Space is the island grid plus the recursion depth.

fast.takeaway: Marking cells as claimed is what makes it linear. Each cell is entered by a flood at most once, so floods never repeat each other's work.

stages.title: Nothing claimed
stages.note: Make a grid of island numbers, all 0. A cell with 0 has not been claimed by any island yet.

stages.title: New island found
stages.note: Land with number 0 must belong to an island we have not seen. Count one more and start a flood there.

stages.title: Flood and claim
stages.note: Write the island number on the cell, then do the same for its four neighbours. Water, claimed cells and edges stop the flood.

stages.title: Return the count
stages.note: One count was added per flood. When the scan ends, that count is the number of islands.

edges.title: All water
edges.why: No land means no flood ever starts. The count stays 0.

edges.title: Diagonal neighbours
edges.why: Only up, down, left and right join cells. A diagonal does not, so these are two islands.

edges.title: Winding island
edges.input: a snake of land that turns several times
edges.why: The flood follows every turn. One start cell is enough, so you must not count each bend as new.

edges.title: Empty map
edges.why: There are no rows, so the first row cannot be read. Check the row count before you take the width.

gotchas.text: new Array(rows).fill(new Array(cols).fill(0)) puts the same inner array in every row. Claiming one cell would claim a whole column. Build rows with Array.from({ length: rows }, () => new Array(cols).fill(0)).
Cells are strings. land[r][c] === 1 is never true for "1". Compare with '1'. A truthiness test is also wrong, because "0" is a non-empty string and counts as true.
make([][]int, rows) gives rows nil slices. Allocate each row with make([]int, cols) before writing, or the first write panics.
A closure that calls itself must be declared first: var flood func(r, c, id int), then assigned. Writing flood := func... cannot refer to flood inside its own body.
Recursion goes as deep as the island is long. A big all-land map can overflow the stack. An explicit queue or stack avoids it, and the idea stays the same.

recap.key: Scan every cell. When you meet unclaimed land, add one to the count and flood it so its whole island is claimed.
recap.complexity: Time O(rows x cols). Space O(rows x cols).
moves: Make a claimed grid, all empty
On unclaimed land: count one and flood its island
